cells.tense: You are standing here holding the last piece of a long build in your hands.
cells.act: carry your own share, all of it
cells.ask: Carry the last piece of one long build without help this week, all of it — not because asking is wrong, but so your own hands feel the close.
cells.core:
When a long job is nearly done, the closing weight is carried better on your own reserves than on borrowed hands. That isn't pride; it's the last stretch of an internal strength that has held through the whole build. You can bring the work to its finish without forcing it to be finished. Holding the weight and letting the thing hold its own shape at once is the balance here.

There's more of the same strength for the next stage of the close, and it comes from your side. Finish the small thing that is only yours to finish, and the close that comes is the one you can stand on. A hand lent now will still be there afterwards, and it won't have to be paid back.
cells.sheetLine: You can bring this in to a close on your own reserves.
cells.verb: Bringing a long effort through to a form that stands on its own.
cells.place: Where a finished thing is tied off and let stand alone.

cells.tense: You are living half in a completion that has not arrived and may never arrive in the shape you've cast it.
cells.ask: Clear one evening this week — no plans, hands free — and let what shows up show up before you decide what it means.
cells.core:
You're building toward a future with a shape you can't actually write, and the effort is starting to arrive before the thing that would justify it. More force stops helping here — it just gets you to the finish line you've already drawn, and the picture has now decided what the work is allowed to mean.

Open before anything has arrived. Clear a stretch of time this week, nothing planned, nothing held, and let whatever shows up show up before you name it. The work doesn't need to be less; it needs a place to land that isn't already framed. What you're making may turn out to be better than the picture, and the picture has been running the room.
cells.sheetLine: You've cast a future before the work can show its own.
cells.verb: Bringing a long effort through to a form that stands on its own.
cells.place: Where a finished thing is tied off and let stand alone.

cells.tense: Something you were bringing to a close has already ended, and you are still standing at the door.
cells.act: see the thing as if for the first time
cells.ask: Fix your attention on one plain object — a table, a street, your own hands — and watch it as if you'd just met it.
cells.core:
The close hasn't happened yet because the contact hasn't happened. There's an old picture of what the finish should be, and the actual thing near you doesn't match it, so it doesn't get picked up. You're standing at a door that has already been passed through.

The way back is small: see the thing as if for the first time. Pick one plain object and watch it as something you've just met, before your mind says what it is. The clear sight pulls the strength back into the place it left; effort into it directly is wasted, and sight is not. Stop there. The next step is already there, and it starts where you're standing.
cells.sheetLine: You've gone on holding the picture of a finish that's already passed.
cells.verb: Bringing a long effort through to a form that stands on its own.
cells.place: Where a finished thing is tied off and let stand alone.

cells.tense: A finished thing is yours and you are telling the room it built itself.
cells.act: describe what is in front of your eyes in five plain lines, no conclusions
cells.ask: Write five plain lines about the finished thing you made — what it is, what it does — no praise, no verdict, nothing about whether it counts.
cells.core:
You brought something through to a standing form, and the picture you've been standing next to still says you didn't. The work is complete; the record of who did it hasn't been written, and the person keeping the record is already inside the room. Naming it has been harder than doing it.

Do the simpler version: look before you interpret. Take the finished thing and describe what meets your eyes in five plain lines — what it is, what it does, no conclusions. Sit with the page. The line that matters here is the one that says what's there, not what it proves. The close belongs to the one who wrote it, and the plain account doesn't have to argue.
